{#qwop} ⟨待采纳·删除·张教授⟩ In the present study, we found that anlotinib enhanced radiosensitivity in vitro and in vivo. ops.markdown: The optimal dose of antiangiogenic agents contributes to improving TIME [@w:w18]. Anlotinib (3 mg/kg) has been shown to boost the antitumor efficacy of radioimmunotherapy [@w:w19], but its dose effect on TIME was not explored. In our study, anlotinib (3 mg/kg) plus radiation did not increase CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell percentage versus IR alone (Supplementary Fig. 8), whereas anlotinib (1.5 mg/kg) reportedly breaks through the immunosuppressive barrier to potentiate TIME [@w:w20]. Consistently, low-dose (1.5 mg/kg) anlotinib plus IR normalized blood vessels (Supplementary Fig. 9), and this dose was therefore selected for subsequent experiments. Nevertheless, the optimal anlotinib dose remains controversial and requires further study.

{#cchj} Reportedly, poorly immunogenic tumors have little response to immunotherapy. LLC is a highly aggressive and poorly immunogenic tumor model that is barely responsive to antitumor immunotherapy [@w:w16]. LLC-OVA, more immunogenic than LLC, remains resistant to immunotherapy [@w:w17]. In the current study, only tumor growth was delayed and exhausted T cells decreased in the radioimmunotherapy group compared to IR alone, whereas CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell proliferation and immune memory activation were not increased. Moreover, the decrease in Foxp3 expression was not observed in the radioimmunotherapy group compared to IR alone (Supplementary Fig. 7). These findings indicated that radioimmunotherapy could not sufficiently activate antitumor immunity. Conversely, triple therapy significantly reduced CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell exhaustion and tumor-infiltrating Tregs, and potentiated proliferation, activation, and immune memory of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells. Taken together, triple therapy maximally improved TIME compared to other regimens.

{#sah9} # Introduction

{#zbbh} Lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer (11.6%) in men and women and remains the primary cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide . Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for about 85% of all lung cancer cases [@w:w1]. Radiotherapy (RT) plays a significant role in NSCLC treatment. However, radiation resistance and high local failure rate are still the major limitations regarding patient prognosis [@w:w2]. The development of immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) treatment makes RT combined with ICB a promising treatment option, but the synergistic effect remains clinically unsatisfactory [@w:w3]. Therefore, finding safe combination strategies to enhance the antitumor efficacy of radiation is an urgent requirement.

{#k77m} Typically, ionizing radiation (IR) induces DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) that directly kills tumor cells. Recently, an increasing number of studies demonstrate that radiation induces double-strand DNA (dsDNA) production and activates cGAS/STING pathway, thereby stimulating innate immunity [@w:w4]. In addition, RT has opposing effects on the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). For example, radiation triggers the DNA damage response (DDR) pathway, upregulates the expression of PD-L1 and forms a suppressive TIME, which leads to RT resistance [@w:w5].
